$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ is false. Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}v-u \\ u+v-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-u+v \\ u+v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$

- Statement $det(A)=-2$ is true. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 1=-2.
$$

- Statement “The transformation $T$ is orientation-preserving” is false. Since $det(A)<0,$ the affine transformation $T$ is not orientation-preserving.

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}v-u \\ u+v\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-u+v \\ u+v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}=(-1)\cdot 1-1\cdot 1=-2\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{1}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}u-2 \\ u-v+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}u \\ u-v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot (-1)-0\cdot 1=-1\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{2}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3u+6v \\ u+2v-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3u+6v \\ u+2v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}=3\cdot 2-6\cdot 1=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{3}$ is *not* invertible.

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta.
$$

Using the fact that $r=-2\cos\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

where we used the identity $\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta.$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta).$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =(-2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =-2\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )}^{′} \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot 2) \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

> *Suppose that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma$. The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n$, the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as*
> $\overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$.

Moreover, if we define

$$
X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

then, by the properties of mean and variance, we have

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = n\mu, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = n\sigma^2
$$

and consequently,

$$
X\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2)
$$

The expected value and the variance of a uniform random variable $X_i \sim U[a,b]$ can be found as

$$
\textrm{E}[X_i] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X_i] = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
n &= 110, \\
μ &= E[X_{i}] \\
&= \frac{a + b}{2} \\
&= \frac{1 + 5}{2} \\
&= \frac{6}{2} \\
&= 3, \\
σ^{2} &= Var[X_{i}] \\
&= ((b - a)^{2})/(12) \\
&= ((5 - 1)^{2})/(12) \\
&= \frac{16}{12} \\
&= \frac{4}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, for the approximate distribution of $X$, we obtain

$$
X \mid ∼N(nμ, nσ^{2}); ∼N(110 \cdot 3, 110 \cdot \frac{4}{3}); ∼N(330, \frac{440}{3})
$$" "Recall that the central limit theorem states the following:

$$
X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

The sample mean $\overline{X}$ is given by

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
n\cdot \overline{X} =\sum_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

Therefore, our random variable $X$ is simply the product of $n$ with the sample mean:

$$
X = n\cdot \overline{X}
$$

Now, the central limit theorem (CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n$, the distribution of $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
$$

Therefore, since

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline X] = \mu, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\overline X] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}
$$

we can calculate $\textrm E[X]$ and $\textrm{Var}[X]$ using the properties of mean and variance as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X] &= E[nX^(―)] \\
&= n \cdot E[X^(―)] \\
&= nμ \\
Var[X] &= Var[nX^(―)] \\
&= n^{2} \cdot Var[X^(―)] \\
&= n^{2} \cdot \frac{σ^{2}}{n} \\
&= nσ^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\overline{X}$ is (approximately) normally distributed, we have that $X$ is also approximately normal. Therefore,

$$
X\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2)
$$

This is an important result. It tells us that provided that we have a sufficiently large I.I.D. sample, the sum of the elements from that sample is approximately normally distributed with mean $n\mu$ and variance $n\sigma^2$. $$"] [:db/cas 17592186189391 :tutorial/content "So, it seems that the curve $r = 1+\cos\theta$ has a horizontal tangent at $\theta = \pi.$ However, to be sure of this, we need to check that the tangent lines flatten out as we approach $\theta = \pi.$ In other words, we need to check that

 

$$
\lim\limits_{\theta \to \pi} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = 0.

Let's now verify that this is true:

Using techniques discussed in previous lessons, it's straightforward to show that

$$
x'(\theta)=-\sin\theta(2\cos\theta+1), \qquad 
y'(\theta)=2\cos^2\theta +\cos\theta - 1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1}{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1)}\right) \\  & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1)}\right) \\  & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\right).\end{aligned}
$$

We already know that substituting $\theta = \pi$ gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac00,$ so evaluating this limit by direct substitution won't work. However, we can evaluate this limit using L'Hopital's rule.

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{(2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)^{′}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′}}\right) \\  & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi } \\  & =\frac{4\cdot (-1)\cdot (0)+0}{2\cdot 1+(-1)} \\  & =\frac{0}{1} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since

$$
\lim\limits_{\theta \to \pi} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = 0
$$

we conclude that our curve does indeed have a horizontal tangent at $\theta = \pi.$

In cases like this, the random variable

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \overline{Y}- (\mu_x - \mu_y)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{S_x^2}{n_x} + \dfrac{S_y^2}{n_y}}}
$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution $T_k$ with $k$ degrees of freedom, where

- $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{Y}$ are the sample means,
- $\mu_x$ and $\mu_y$ are the population means,
- $n_x$ and $n_y$ are the sample sizes, and
- $S_x^2$ and $S_y^2$ are the sample variances.

In our example:

- $H_0: \mu_x = \mu_y$ is the null hypothesis
- $H_1: \mu_x < \mu_y$ is the alternative (one-tailed) hypothesis

We can estimate the number of degrees of freedom $k$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
k &= min(15 - 1, 16 - 1) \\
&= min(14, 15) \\
&= 14
\end{aligned}
$$

Assuming the null hypothesis, i.e.

$$
\mu_x - \mu_y = 0
$$

we compute the test statistic:

$$
\begin{aligned}
t &= (x^(―) - y^(―) - (μ_{x} - μ_{y}))/(\sqrt{\frac{s_{x}^{2}}{n_{x}} + \frac{s_{y}^{2}}{n_{y}}}) \\
&= (30 - 31 - (0))/(\sqrt{\frac{1^{2}}{15} + \frac{3^{2}}{16}}) \\
&\approx - 1.261
\end{aligned}
$$

According to the table, the $1\%$ one-tailed critical value for $k = 14$ degrees of freedom is

$$
t \approx 2.624
$$

- The value of $k$ that we pick should give a multiple of $10a_0$ when combined with the existing $a_0$ term. This allows us to factor $10$ from the left-hand side.

With this in mind, note that

$$
a_0+3\cdot 13 a_0 = a_0+39 a_0 = 40a_0
$$

> Now, without changing the congruence, we can add $39a_0$ to the left-hand side since it's congruent to $0$ modulo $13{:}$

$$

Next, we cancel out the factor of $10$.

> Since $10$ and $13$ are coprime, we can use a division rule for congruences and cancel out the factor of $10$ to get
> $10^{n - 1}a_{n} + ⋯ + 10a_{2} + a_{1} + 4a_{0} \mid ≡0 \mid (mod13)$.

$$

$$

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \, \mathrm d x \, \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v))  \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \mathrm d u \, \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u = 4x + 2y, \qquad v = y - x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

$$
\mathbf{T}^{-1}:{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]} \to {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u ( x , y ) \\ v ( x , y )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 3\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

> *An integer is divisible $3$ if and only if the sum of the digits is divisible by $3$.*

For example, we can use this rule to check that $2\,387\,465\,652$ is divisible by $3$. The sum of the digits is given by

$$
2+3+8+7+4+6+5+6+5+2 = 48
$$

and $48$ is divisible by $3$. Therefore, $2\,387\,465\,652$ is divisible by $3$.

These rules may have seemed mysterious when you first studied them. However, we can prove them using the properties of modular congruence!

To demonstrate, let's prove the "is divisible by $3$" rule.

First, let $N$ be a positive integer. We'll express $N$ in expanded form as follows:

$$
N = 10^{n}a_{n} + \cdots + 10^{2}a_{2} + 10a_{1} + a_0
$$

Here, $a_{n}, \ldots, a_2, a_{1}, a_{0}$ are the digits of the number.

We wish to prove the following statement:

$$
3 \mid N \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad 3 \mid \big(a_{n} + \cdots + a_{2} + a_{1} + a_0 \big)
$$

First, we write the statement in terms of congruences:

> *According to the definition of modular congruence,*
> $3 \mid N \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad N \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:3)$.

Now, let's expand the left-hand side:

> *Expressing $N$ in expanded form, we get*
> $10^{n}a_{n} + ⋯ + 10^{2}a_{2} + 10a_{1} + a_{0} \mid ≡0 \mid (mod3)$.

Next, we need to show that this implies

$$
a_{n} + ⋯ + a_{2} + a_{1} + a_{0}≡0 \mid (mod3)
$$

To do this, recall the multiplication properties of modular arithmetic:

- For any $k\in \mathbb N$, we have $a \equiv b \:\Leftrightarrow\: a^k\equiv b^k \quad (\textrm{mod}\: n)$.
- For any $c\in \mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$, we have $a \equiv b \:\Leftrightarrow\: ac \equiv bc \quad (\textrm{mod}\: n)$.

With this in mind, note that
$10 \equiv 1 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad 10^k a_k \equiv 1^k a_k \qquad (\textrm{mod}\: 3)$.

So, we proceed as follows:

> *Now, without changing the congruence, we can swap each occurrence of $10$ with $1$ on the left-hand side since they're congruent modulo $3{:}$*
> $$
\displaystyle \begin{bmatrix}10^{n}a_{n} + ⋯ + 10^{2}a_{2} + 10a_{1} + a_{0} & ≡0 & (mod3) \\ (1)^{n}a_{n} + ⋯ + (1)^{2}a_{2} + (1)a_{1} + a_{0} & ≡0 & (mod3) \\ a_{n} + ⋯ + a_{2} + a_{1} + a_{0} & ≡0 & (mod3)\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, we can write down that conclusion.

> *Therefore, according to the definition of modular congruence, the final equation means that*
> $3 \mid \big(a_{n} + \cdots + a_{2} + a_{1} + a_0 \big)$.

And we're done!

**Note:** All the transformations we performed above also work in reverse, which means that the right-to-left implication is also true.

We can also use modular congruence to prove slightly more complex divisibility rules. Let's see an example." "You will have learned certain *divisibility tests* early in your mathematical career. One such rule is determining whether a number is divisible by $3$.

$$
M_k = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i^k
$$

In particular, the first and second sample moments are given by

$$
M_1 = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \,, \qquad M_2 = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2
$$

To find the method of moments estimate for a parameter, we calculate a sample moment and the corresponding theoretical moment and equate them.

We are given the sum of the squared values in the sample. So, we can calculate the second sample moment:

$$
m_2 = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 = \dfrac{9}{15}=\dfrac{3}{5}
$$

The variables $X_i$ follow a Bernoulli distribution. Therefore,

$$
\textrm{E}[X_i] = \theta, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X_i] = \theta(1-\theta)
$$

We also have

$$
\textrm{Var}[X_i] = \textrm{E}[X^2_i] - \left(\textrm{E}[X_i]\right)^2
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the second theoretical moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X_{i}^{2}] &= Var[X_{i}] + (E[X_{i}])^{2} \\
&= θ(1 - θ) + θ^{2} \\
&= θ - θ^{2} + θ^{2} \\
&= θ
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, equating the sample and theoretical first moments, using the estimator $\widehat\theta_{MM}$ in place of $\theta$, we get the following estimate for $\theta{:}$

$$
M_k = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i^k
$$

In particular, the first and second sample moments are given by

$$
M_1 = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \,, \qquad M_2 = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2
$$

To find the method of moments estimator for a parameter, we calculate a sample moment and the corresponding theoretical moment and equate them.

We are given the sum of the squared values in the sample. So, we can calculate the second sample moment:

$$
m_2 = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 = \dfrac{140}{5}=28
$$

We are given that the variables follow a uniform distribution $U(a,b)$. Therefore,

$$
\textrm{E}[X_i] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X_i] = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}
$$

We also have

$$
\textrm{Var}[X_i] = \textrm{E}[X^2_i] - \left(\textrm{E}[X_i]\right)^2
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the second theoretical moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X_{i}^{2}] &= Var[X_{i}] + (E[X_{i}])^{2} \\
&= (((θ + 6) - θ)^{2})/(12) + ((θ + (θ + 6))/(2))^{2} \\
&= \frac{36}{12} + (θ + 3)^{2} \\
&= 3 + θ^{2} + 6θ + 9 \\
&= θ^{2} + 6θ + 12
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the sample and theoretical second moments and using the estimator $\widehat\theta_{MM}$ in place of $\theta$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{θ}_{MM}^{2} + 6\widehat{θ}_{MM} + 12 &= 28
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve for $\widehat\theta_{MM}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{θ}_{MM}^{2} + 6\widehat{θ}_{MM} + 12 &= 28 \\
\widehat{θ}_{MM}^{2} + 6\widehat{θ}_{MM} - 16 &= 0 \\
(\widehat{θ}_{MM} + 8)(\widehat{θ}_{MM} - 2) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solutions

$$
\widehat{\theta}_{MM}= -8, \qquad \widehat{\theta}_{MM}= 2
$$

However, we discard the negative solution since we are given that $\theta > 0$. Therefore, our method of moments estimate for $\theta$ is

$$
\widehat{\theta}_{MM}= \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2}

$$

$$

&= \frac{80}{2} \\
&= 40
\end{aligned}
$$

In this lesson, we extend this idea to functions where the input is a *matrix* and the output is a scalar.

Suppose we have a function $f: \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} \to \mathbb{R}$ that maps a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ to a scalar value $f(A)$. Just like with vector inputs, we define the **gradient of $f$ with respect to $A$** as the matrix of partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to each individual entry of $A{:}$

$$
\nabla_A f(A) = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cccc}{\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{11}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{12}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{1 n}}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{21}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{22}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{2 n}}} \\ \vdots  & \vdots  & \ddots  & \vdots  \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{m 1}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{m 2}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{m n}}}\end{array} \right]}
$$

This gradient has the same shape as the matrix $A.$ It tells us how sensitive the output $f(A)$ is to changes in each element $a_{ij}$.

Let’s apply this to a concrete example. Suppose we define the function

$$
f(X) = \ln(\det(X))
$$

for a square matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}$. Let's find the gradient of $f$ with respect to $X$ and evaluate it at a specific point.

First, we write the matrix $X$ as
$$
X = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{x}_{11} & {x}_{12} \\ {x}_{21} & {x}_{22}\end{array} \right]}.
$$
Then, the determinant of $X$ is

$$
\det(X) = x_{11}x_{22} - x_{12}x_{21}.
$$

So, the function becomes

$$
f(X) = \ln(x_{11}x_{22} - x_{12}x_{21}).
$$

For example, suppose we have two numbers $a$ and $b$ such that

$$
1\leq a \leq 12\qquad\text{and}\qquad 4\leq b \leq 8
$$

What is the largest possible value of $a - b$?

We can answer this question by applying the following principle:

> *To **maximize** the difference of two numbers $a$ and $b$, we take the **largest possible** value of $a$ and subtract the **smallest possible** value of $b$.*

Take a moment to appreciate why this must be true. If we're trying to maximize a difference, we want to start with the largest number possible and then subtract as little as possible from it.

So, let's compute the largest possible value of $a$, the smallest possible value of $b$, and find their difference:

- Since $1\leq a \leq 12$, the largest possible value of $a$ is $12$.
$\max(a) = 12$
- Since $4\leq b \leq 8$, the smallest possible value of $b$ is $4$.
$\min(b) = 4$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
max(a - b) &= max(a) - min(b) \\
&= 12 - 4 \\
&= 8
\end{aligned}
$$

The rule for maximizing a *quotient* is similar, though it only works for positive numbers:

> *To **maximize** the quotient of two **positive** numbers $a$ and $b$, we take the **largest possible** value of $a$ and divide by the **smallest possible** value of $b$.*

Again, take a moment to appreciate why this must be true. We want the dividend to be as large as possible, while the divisor should be as small as possible.

So, in this example, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
max\left(\frac{a}{b}\right) &= (max(a))/(min(b)) \\
&= \frac{12}{4} \\
&= 3
\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =7(0.5)^{4}-2(0.5)^{5} \\  & =7\cdot 0.062\,5-2\cdot 0.031\,25 \\  & =0.375.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
{k}^{p+1}={2}^{p+1}.

$$

$$

$$

$$

- $b(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}({e}^{t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{t})^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot {e}^{t}+1\cdot {e}^{t} \\ 1\cdot {e}^{t}+2\cdot {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- $c(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{3t} \\ 5{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{is}$ also a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$

Now, consider the set of solutions ${a,c}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(a,c) & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{3t} & 5{e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t} & 5{e}^{3t}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =({e}^{3t})(5{e}^{3t})-(5{e}^{3t})({e}^{3t}) \\  & =5{e}^{6t}-5{e}^{6t} \\  & =0,\end{aligned}

which is zero for all $t\in R.$ Thus, since $a$ and $c$ are both solutions of the same linear system, but their Wronskian is identically zero, they are linearly dependent and do **not** form a fundamental set of solutions of the system." The **order** of a numerical method describes how fast these errors shrink as $\Delta x$ decreases.
A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the *largest positive* integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^p\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0.
$$

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately $k^p{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}e\left(\frac{Δx}{k}\right) & ≈K{\left(\frac{Δx}{k}\right)}^{p}=\frac{K(Δx)^{p}}{{k}^{p}}≈\frac{e(Δx)}{{k}^{p}}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's demonstrate with an example. Suppose a numerical method is used to approximate the solution to an initial value problem.

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.21,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.21) = 0.785.$

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.07,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.07) = 0.010.$

Using this data, we can estimate the order of the numerical method.

The step size decreases from $0.21$ to $0.07.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k = \dfrac{0.21}{0.07} = 3.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the GTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
k^p = 3^p.
$$

On the other hand, the GTE actually decreases from $0.785$ to $0.010.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\dfrac{0.785}{0.010} = 78.5.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the GTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{p} & ≈78.5 \\ p & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(78.5) \\ p & ≈3.97….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the approximate order of the method is $4.$

But why is order important? Well, a higher order means that the error decreases faster as $\Delta x$ decreases. As a result, higher-order methods can achieve a target accuracy *with fewer steps*. In this way, order predicts the accuracy you gain when you make steps smaller." We do this by converting the $2L$-periodic function into a $2\pi$-periodic one using a change of variables.

Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in[-L,L)$ to $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
To use the standard $2\pi$-period Fourier formulas, define

$$
s=\frac{\pi}{L}x
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
g(s)=f\!\left(\frac{L}{\pi}s\right).
$$

Then $g$ is $2\pi$-periodic.

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $g$, the Fourier series is

$$
g(s)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl(a_n\cos(ns)+b_n\sin(ns)\bigr),
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,ds, \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1, \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Coefficients $b_n$ (for $n \geq 1$) and $a_0$ can be found similarly.

$$
y''(x)+P(x)y'(x)+Q(x)y=0,\qquad a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
\alpha_{1}y(a)+\beta_{1}y'(a)=0,\qquad
\alpha_{2}y(b)+\beta_{2}y'(b)=0,
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and $\alpha_i, \beta_i$ are real constants such that $(\alpha_i,\beta_i)\ne(0,0).$ Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x).$  

Now, let's define the following matrix:

$$
A=
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\alpha }_{1} {y}_{1} ( a ) + {\beta }_{1} {y}_{1}^{\prime } ( a ) & {\alpha }_{1} {y}_{2} ( a ) + {\beta }_{1} {y}_{2}^{\prime } ( a ) \\ {\alpha }_{2} {y}_{1} ( b ) + {\beta }_{2} {y}_{1}^{\prime } ( b ) & {\alpha }_{2} {y}_{2} ( b ) + {\beta }_{2} {y}_{2}^{\prime } ( b )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y\equiv0$ if and only if $\det(A)\ne0.$
In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions.  So, setting $\alpha_i=0,$ $\beta_i=1,$ $a=1,$ and $b=3,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{y}_{1}^{\prime } ( 1 ) & {y}_{2}^{\prime } ( 1 ) \\ {y}_{1}^{\prime } ( 3 ) & {y}_{2}^{\prime } ( 3 )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y=e^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-2m-3 & =0 \\ (m-3)(m+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=3$ and $m=-1,$ and so the fundamental solutions are

$$
y_{1}(x)=e^{3x}\;\textrm{and}\;y_{2}(x)=e^{-x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
y_1'(x) = 3e^{3x}, \qquad y_2'(x) = -e^{-x}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3(1)} & -{e}^{-1} \\ 3{e}^{3(3)} & -{e}^{-3}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3} & -{e}^{-1} \\ 3{e}^{9} & -{e}^{-3}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =(3{e}^{3})(-{e}^{-3})-(-{e}^{-1})(3{e}^{9}) \\  & =-3+3{e}^{8} \\  & =3({e}^{8}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(A)\ne0,$ we conclude that this BVP has the unique trivial solution $y\equiv0.$" "Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

$$
y''(x) + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = f(x), \qquad a \leq x \leq b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
\alpha_1 y(a) + \beta_1 y'(a) = \gamma_1, \qquad 
\alpha_2 y(b) + \beta_2 y'(b) = \gamma_2
$$

where $P, Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ are real constants such that $(\alpha_i, \beta_i) \neq (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y \equiv 0.$ Specifically:

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y \equiv 0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem either has no solution or a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

$$
A = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}\hspace{0.167em} {\alpha }_{1} {y}_{1} ( a ) + {\beta }_{1} {y}_{1}^{\prime } ( a ) & {\alpha }_{1} {y}_{2} ( a ) + {\beta }_{1} {y}_{2}^{\prime } ( a ) \\ {\alpha }_{2} {y}_{1} ( b ) + {\beta }_{2} {y}_{1}^{\prime } ( b ) & {\alpha }_{2} {y}_{2} ( b ) + {\beta }_{2} {y}_{2}^{\prime } ( b )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y \equiv 0$ if and only if $\det(A) \neq 0.$ In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions. So, setting $\alpha_i = 0, \beta_i = 1, a = 0,$ and $b = \pi,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{y}_{1}^{\prime } ( 0 ) & {y}_{2}^{\prime } ( 0 ) \\ {y}_{1}^{\prime } ( \pi  ) & {y}_{2}^{\prime } ( \pi  )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y = e^{m x}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m = \pm 4\textrm i.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
y_1(x) = \cos 4x, \qquad y_2(x) = \sin 4x.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
y_1'(x) = -4\sin 4x, \qquad y_2'(x) = 4\cos 4x.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot 0) & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot 0) \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \pi ) & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \pi )\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(A)| & =|0\cdot 4-4\cdot 0| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(A) = 0,$ the corresponding homogeneous BVP $\textrm{has infinitely many solutions}.$

Therefore, since the corresponding homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, our inhomogeneous BVP $\textrm{has infinitely many solutions or no solution}.$" "Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}-3y\} & =L\{2{u}_{\pi /2}(t)\cdot sin\,(2t-\pi )\} \\ L\{{y}^{′}\}-3L\{y\} & =L\{2{u}_{\pi /2}(t)\cdot sin\,(2t-\pi )\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $\mathcal L\left\{y' \right\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=-2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{y' \right\}  = sY(s) - y(0)   = sY(s) + 2
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
2u_{\pi/2}(t)\cdot \sin\!\left(2t-\pi\right)
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $f(t)=2\sin(2t-\pi).$ This can be interpreted as time-delayed sinusoidal forcing. 

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
\mathcal L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\} = e^{-as} \cdot \mathcal L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

$$

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5u-2v-5 \\ 10u-4v+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5u-2v \\ 10u-4v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}5 & -2 \\ 10 & -4\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}5 & -2 \\ 10 & -4\end{vmatrix}=-4\cdot 5-(-2)\cdot 10=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{1}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v-4 \\ u+5v+7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v \\ u+5v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5\end{vmatrix}=5\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot 1=6\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{2}$ is invertible.

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 6\end{vmatrix}=6\cdot 2-4\cdot 3=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{3}$ is *not* invertible.

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{1}{3}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $sin⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $cos⁡\theta =\frac{1}{3}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{9}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{8}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Knowing that $csc⁡\theta =\frac{1}{sin⁡\theta },$ we have

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}csc⁡\theta  & =\frac{3}{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{2\sqrt{2}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2\cdot 2} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\end{aligned}

$$

$$
Q{Q}^{T}={Q}^{T}Q=I.
$$

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

- For any orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we have ${Q}^{-1}={Q}^{T}.$

- $(AB)^{T}={B}^{T}{A}^{T}$ for conformable matrices $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the statements in turn.

- Statement “If $\lambda $ is a real eigenvalue of $Q,$ then $\lambda =\pm 1$” is true. If $\lambda $ is an eigenvalue of an orthogonal matrix $Q$ then $\lambda =\pm 1$

- Statement “If the determinant of $P$ is either $1$ or $-1,$ then $P$ is orthogonal” is false. Every orthogonal matrix has the determinant equal to $\pm 1$, but not every matrix with the determinant equal to $\pm 1$ is orthogonal. As a counterexample, consider the following matrix:

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The determinant of $P$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}det(P)=2\cdot 1-1\cdot 1=1,\end{aligned}
$$

 however, $P$ is not orthogonal since, for example, the first column is not normalized.

- Statement “$Q-I$ is singular” is false. As a counterexample, consider the following orthogonal matrix:

$$
Q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}
$$

We have that

$$

$$

and $Q-I$ is not singular since, for example, it doesn't have proportional rows or columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is “If $\lambda $ is a real eigenvalue of $Q,$ then $\lambda =\pm 1$” only." "Recall that a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta.
$$

Using the fact that $r=-2\cos\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\end{aligned}

where we used the identity $\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta.$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =(-2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =-2\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}

$$

> *Suppose that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma$. The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n$, the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as*
> $\overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$.

Moreover, if we define

$$
X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

then, by the properties of mean and variance, we have

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = n\mu, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = n\sigma^2
$$

and consequently,

$$
X\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2)
$$

The expected value and the variance of a uniform random variable $X_i \sim U[a,b]$ can be found as

$$
\textrm{E}[X_i] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X_i] = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
n &= 110, \\
μ &= E[X_{i}] \\
&= \frac{a + b}{2} \\
&= \frac{1 + 5}{2} \\
&= \frac{6}{2} \\
&= 3, \\
σ^{2} &= Var[X_{i}] \\
&= ((b - a)^{2})/(12) \\
&= ((5 - 1)^{2})/(12) \\
&= \frac{16}{12} \\
&= \frac{4}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta_0)}{x'(\theta_0)}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
y'(\theta_0) \neq 0 \qquad \textrm{and}\qquad x'(\theta_0) = 0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at $\theta_0$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\dfrac00$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
\lim\limits_{\theta \to \theta_0^{-}} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \pm\infty \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \lim\limits_{\theta \to \theta_0^{+}} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \pm\infty.
$$

In this case, we're told that $y'\left(\dfrac\pi2\right)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta = \dfrac\pi2$ into the expression for $x'(\theta),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+2\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\operatorname{csc}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)) \\  & =0\cdot (0+2\cdot 0\cdot 1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

The sample mean $\overline{X}$ is given by

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
n\cdot \overline{X} =\sum_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

Therefore, our random variable $X$ is simply the product of $n$ with the sample mean:

$$
X = n\cdot \overline{X}
$$

Now, the central limit theorem (CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n$, the distribution of $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
$$

Therefore, since

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline X] = \mu, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\overline X] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}
$$

we can calculate $\textrm E[X]$ and $\textrm{Var}[X]$ using the properties of mean and variance as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X] &= E[nX^(―)] \\
&= n \cdot E[X^(―)] \\
&= nμ \\
Var[X] &= Var[nX^(―)] \\
&= n^{2} \cdot Var[X^(―)] \\
&= n^{2} \cdot \frac{σ^{2}}{n} \\
&= nσ^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\overline{X}$ is (approximately) normally distributed, we have that $X$ is also approximately normal. Therefore,

$$
X\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2)
$$

This is an important result. It tells us that provided that we have a sufficiently large I.I.D. sample, the sum of the elements from that sample is approximately normally distributed with mean $n\mu$ and variance $n\sigma^2$. This result does not depend on the distribution of the $X_i$'s!" In cases like this, the random variable

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \overline{Y}- (\mu_x - \mu_y)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{S_x^2}{n_x} + \dfrac{S_y^2}{n_y}}}
$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution $T_k$ with $k$ degrees of freedom, where

- $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{Y}$ are the sample means,
- $\mu_x$ and $\mu_y$ are the population means,
- $n_x$ and $n_y$ are the sample sizes, and
- $S_x^2$ and $S_y^2$ are the sample variances.

In our example:

- $H_0: \mu_x = \mu_y$ is the null hypothesis
- $H_1: \mu_x < \mu_y$ is the alternative (one-tailed) hypothesis

We can estimate the number of degrees of freedom $k$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
k &= min(15 - 1, 16 - 1) \\
&= min(14, 15) \\
&= 14
\end{aligned}
$$

Assuming the null hypothesis, i.e.

$$
\mu_x - \mu_y = 0
$$

we compute the test statistic:

$$
\begin{aligned}
t &= (x^(―) - y^(―) - (μ_{x} - μ_{y}))/(\sqrt{\frac{s_{x}^{2}}{n_{x}} + \frac{s_{y}^{2}}{n_{y}}}) \\
&= (30 - 31 - (0))/(\sqrt{\frac{1^{2}}{15} + \frac{3^{2}}{16}}) \\
&\approx - 1.261
\end{aligned}
$$

According to the table, the $1\%$ one-tailed critical value for $k = 14$ degrees of freedom is

$$
t \approx 2.624
$$

$$

$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

$$

$$

$$"] [:db/cas 17592186199559 :tutorial/content "The **minimum** of a set $S$ is the element $x_{\min} \in S$ such that 

$$
x_{\min} \leq x
$$

for all $x \in S.$ In other words, the minimum is the element of $S$ that is *smaller than or equal to* any other element.

Similarly, the **maximum** of a set $S$ is the element $x_{\max} \in S$ such that 

$$
x \leq x_{\max}
$$

for all $x \in S.$ In other words, the maximum is the element of $S$ that is *larger than or equal to* any other element.

For example, what are the minimum and maximum of the following set? 

$$
A = \big\{ 2, \: -\sqrt{5}, \: 3, \: -1 \big\}
$$

Note that $-\sqrt{5} \approx -2.236.$ Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}min(A) & =min\{2,\,-\sqrt{5},\,3,\,-1\}=-\sqrt{5} \\ max(A) & =max\{2,\,-\sqrt{5},\,3,\,-1\}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Some sets may not have a maximum or minimum. 

For example, consider the semi-open interval of real numbers $B=[1, 5).$ In this case, we have

$$
\min(B) = \min[1, 5) = 1.
$$

However, since $5 \notin B,$ the set has no maximum!

Finally, note the following:

- The maximum and minimum elements *must* belong to the underlying set.

- If the maximum or minimum elements exist, they are unique. In other words, there can be, at most, only one maximum and only one minimum.

$$

$$

Here, $a_{n}, \ldots, a_2, a_{1}, a_{0}$ are the digits of the number.

We wish to prove the following statement:

$$
3 \mid N \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad 3 \mid \big(a_{n} + \cdots + a_{2} + a_{1} + a_0 \big)
$$

First, we write the statement in terms of congruences:

> *According to the definition of modular congruence,*
> $3 \mid N \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad N \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:3)$.

$$
M_1 = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \,, \qquad M_2 = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2
$$

To find the method of moments estimate for a parameter, we calculate a sample moment and the corresponding theoretical moment and equate them.

We are given the sum of the squared values in the sample. So, we can calculate the second sample moment:

$$
m_2 = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 = \dfrac{9}{15}=\dfrac{3}{5}
$$

The variables $X_i$ follow a Bernoulli distribution. Therefore,

$$
\textrm{E}[X_i] = \theta, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X_i] = \theta(1-\theta)
$$

We also have

$$
\textrm{Var}[X_i] = \textrm{E}[X^2_i] - \left(\textrm{E}[X_i]\right)^2
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the second theoretical moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X_{i}^{2}] &= Var[X_{i}] + (E[X_{i}])^{2} \\
&= θ(1 - θ) + θ^{2} \\
&= θ - θ^{2} + θ^{2} \\
&= θ
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

We also have

$$

&= 3 + θ^{2} + 6θ + 9 \\
&= θ^{2} + 6θ + 12
\end{aligned}

$$

\widehat{θ}_{MM}^{2} + 6\widehat{θ}_{MM} + 12 &= 28
\end{aligned}

{\left[ \begin{array}{cccc}{\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {x}_{11}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {x}_{12}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {x}_{1 n}}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {x}_{21}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {x}_{22}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {x}_{2 n}}} \\ \vdots  & \vdots  & \ddots  & \vdots  \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {x}_{m 1}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {x}_{m 2}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {x}_{m n}}}\end{array} \right]}.

$$
f(X) = (\det(X))^2 = (x_{11}x_{22} - x_{12}x_{21})^2.
$$

So, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,{∇}_{X}f(X) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{11}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{12}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{21}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{22}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{11}}({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})^{2} & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{12}}({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})^{2} \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{21}}({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})^{2} & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{22}}({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})\cdot {x}_{22} & 2({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})\cdot (-{x}_{21}) \\ 2({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})\cdot (-{x}_{12}) & 2({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})\cdot {x}_{11}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =2({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{22} & -{x}_{21} \\ -{x}_{12} & {x}_{11}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =2det(X)\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{22} & -{x}_{21} \\ -{x}_{12} & {x}_{11}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

&= 40
\end{aligned}
$$

In this lesson, we extend this idea to functions where the input is a *matrix* and the output is a scalar.

Suppose we have a function $f: \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} \to \mathbb{R}$ that maps a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ to a scalar value $f(A)$. Just like with vector inputs, we define the **gradient of $f$ with respect to $A$** as the matrix of partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to each individual entry of $A{:}$

$$
\nabla_A f(A) = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cccc}{\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{11}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{12}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{1 n}}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{21}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{22}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{2 n}}} \\ \vdots  & \vdots  & \ddots  & \vdots  \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{m 1}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{m 2}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {a}_{m n}}}\end{array} \right]}
$$

This gradient has the same shape as the matrix $A.$ It tells us how sensitive the output $f(A)$ is to changes in each element $a_{ij}$.

Let’s apply this to a concrete example. Suppose we define the function

$$
f(X) = \ln(\det(X))
$$

for a square matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}$. Let's find the gradient of $f$ with respect to $X$ and evaluate it at a specific point.

First, we write the matrix $X$ as
$$
X = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{x}_{11} & {x}_{12} \\ {x}_{21} & {x}_{22}\end{array} \right]}.
$$
Then, the determinant of $X$ is

$$
\det(X) = x_{11}x_{22} - x_{12}x_{21}.
$$

So, the function becomes

$$
f(X) = \ln(x_{11}x_{22} - x_{12}x_{21}).
$$

To find the gradient, we differentiate $f$ with respect to each element of $X.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{X}f(X) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{11}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{12}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{21}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{22}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{11}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{12}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{21}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{22}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{x}_{22}}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}} & -\frac{{x}_{21}}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}} \\ -\frac{{x}_{12}}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}} & \frac{{x}_{11}}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{22} & -{x}_{21} \\ -{x}_{12} & {x}_{11}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{det(X)}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{22} & -{x}_{21} \\ -{x}_{12} & {x}_{11}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, suppose we wish to evaluate this gradient at
$$
X = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}3 & 1 \\ 5 & - 2\end{array} \right]}.
$$
First, we compute the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(X) & =3\cdot (-2)-1\cdot 5 \\  & =-6-5 \\  & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our values into our gradient. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{X}f(X) & =-\frac{1}{11}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{11}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 5 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

This result tells us how the scalar output $f(X) = \ln(\det(X))$ would change with respect to small changes in each entry of the matrix $X$. For example, suppose we have two numbers $a$ and $b$ such that

$$
1\leq a \leq 12\qquad\text{and}\qquad 4\leq b \leq 8
$$

What is the largest possible value of $a - b$?

We can answer this question by applying the following principle:

> *To **maximize** the difference of two numbers $a$ and $b$, we take the **largest possible** value of $a$ and subtract the **smallest possible** value of $b$.*

Take a moment to appreciate why this must be true. If we're trying to maximize a difference, we want to start with the largest number possible and then subtract as little as possible from it.

So, let's compute the largest possible value of $a$, the smallest possible value of $b$, and find their difference:

- Since $1\leq a \leq 12$, the largest possible value of $a$ is $12$.
$\max(a) = 12$
- Since $4\leq b \leq 8$, the smallest possible value of $b$ is $4$.
$\min(b) = 4$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
max(a - b) &= max(a) - min(b) \\
&= 12 - 4 \\
&= 8
\end{aligned}
$$

The rule for maximizing a *quotient* is similar, though it only works for positive numbers:

> *To **maximize** the quotient of two **positive** numbers $a$ and $b$, we take the **largest possible** value of $a$ and divide by the **smallest possible** value of $b$.*

Again, take a moment to appreciate why this must be true. We want the dividend to be as large as possible, while the divisor should be as small as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}
max\left(\frac{a}{b}\right) &= (max(a))/(min(b)) \\
&= \frac{12}{4} \\

$$
\mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\big\}
= e^{-as}\,\mathcal{L}\big\{g(t+a)\big\},
\qquad \text{for} \; s > s_0,
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{ u(t -4)\,\cos(9\pi t) \right\}.
$$

Therefore, $a=4,$ and we have 

$$
\mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-4)\,g(t)\big\} = e^{-4s}\,\mathcal{L}\big\{g(t+4)\big\},
$$

where $g(t)= \cos(9\pi t).$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+4) & =cos\,(9\pi (t+4)) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(9\pi t+36\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡9\pi t\operatorname{cos}⁡36\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡9\pi t\operatorname{sin}⁡36\pi  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡9\pi t\cdot 1-\operatorname{sin}⁡9\pi t\cdot 0 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡9\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathcal{L} \left\{\cos(\omega t)\right\}=\dfrac{s}{s^2 + \omega^2}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$

$$
e(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^p\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $\Delta x$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately $k^p.$

First, we compute the GTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.4,$ the GTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}e(0.4) & =4(0.4)^{3}+(0.4)^{4} \\  & =4\cdot 0.064+1\cdot 0.025\,6 \\  & =0.256+0.025\,6 \\  & =0.281\,6 \\  & ≈0.282.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.2,$ the GTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}e(0.2) & =4(0.2)^{3}+(0.2)^{4} \\  & =4\cdot 0.008+1\cdot 0.001\,6 \\  & =0.032+0.001\,6 \\  & =0.033\,6 \\  & ≈0.034.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.4$ to $0.2.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k = \dfrac{0.4}{0.2} = 2.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the GTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
k^p = 2^p.
$$

On the other hand, the GTE actually decreases from $0.281\,6$ to $0.033\,6.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\dfrac{0.281\,6}{0.033\,6} = 8.380\,95\ldots \approx  \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gray]{8.381}.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the GTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{p} & ≈8.380\,952… \\ p & ≈{log}_{2}⁡(8.380\,95…) \\ p & ≈3.067….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gray]{3}.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the GTE:

$$
e(\Delta x) = 4(\Delta x)^3 + (\Delta x)^4
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
e(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^3\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $3.$" "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =7(0.5)^{4}-2(0.5)^{5} \\  & =7\cdot 0.062\,5-2\cdot 0.031\,25 \\  & =0.375.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.25) & =7(0.25)^{4}-2(0.25)^{5} \\  & =7\cdot (0.003\,906…)-2\cdot (0.000\,976…) \\  & =0.025\,39… \\  & ≈0.025.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
k=\frac{0.5}{0.25}=2.

$$
{k}^{p+1}={2}^{p+1}.

$$

$$

First, we write our system in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}({e}^{3t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{3t})^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} \\ 3{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot {e}^{3t}+1\cdot {e}^{3t} \\ 1\cdot {e}^{3t}+2\cdot {e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} \\ 3{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} \\ 3{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $b(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}({e}^{t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{t})^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot {e}^{t}+1\cdot {e}^{t} \\ 1\cdot {e}^{t}+2\cdot {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- $c(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{3t} \\ 5{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{is}$ also a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}(5{e}^{3t})^{′} \\ (5{e}^{3t})^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{3t} \\ 5{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}15{e}^{3t} \\ 15{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 5{e}^{3t}+1\cdot 5{e}^{3t} \\ 1\cdot 5{e}^{3t}+2\cdot 5{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}15{e}^{3t} \\ 15{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}15{e}^{3t} \\ 15{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions ${a,c}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(a,c) & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{3t} & 5{e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t} & 5{e}^{3t}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =({e}^{3t})(5{e}^{3t})-(5{e}^{3t})({e}^{3t}) \\  & =5{e}^{6t}-5{e}^{6t} \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which is zero for all $t\in R.$ Thus, since $a$ and $c$ are both solutions of the same linear system, but their Wronskian is identically zero, they are linearly dependent and do **not** form a fundamental set of solutions of the system." The **order** of a numerical method describes how fast these errors shrink as $\Delta x$ decreases.
A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the *largest positive* integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^p\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0.
$$

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately $k^p{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}e\left(\frac{Δx}{k}\right) & ≈K{\left(\frac{Δx}{k}\right)}^{p}=\frac{K(Δx)^{p}}{{k}^{p}}≈\frac{e(Δx)}{{k}^{p}}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's demonstrate with an example. Suppose a numerical method is used to approximate the solution to an initial value problem.

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.21,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.21) = 0.785.$

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.07,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.07) = 0.010.$

Using this data, we can estimate the order of the numerical method.

The step size decreases from $0.21$ to $0.07.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k = \dfrac{0.21}{0.07} = 3.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the GTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
k^p = 3^p.
$$

On the other hand, the GTE actually decreases from $0.785$ to $0.010.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\dfrac{0.785}{0.010} = 78.5.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the GTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{p} & ≈78.5 \\ p & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(78.5) \\ p & ≈3.97….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the approximate order of the method is $4.$

But why is order important? Well, a higher order means that the error decreases faster as $\Delta x$ decreases. As a result, higher-order methods can achieve a target accuracy *with fewer steps*. In this way, order predicts the accuracy you gain when you make steps smaller." We do this by converting the $2L$-periodic function into a $2\pi$-periodic one using a change of variables.

Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in[-L,L)$ to $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
To use the standard $2\pi$-period Fourier formulas, define

$$
s=\frac{\pi}{L}x
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
g(s)=f\!\left(\frac{L}{\pi}s\right).
$$

Then $g$ is $2\pi$-periodic.

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $g$, the Fourier series is

$$
g(s)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl(a_n\cos(ns)+b_n\sin(ns)\bigr),
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,ds, \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1, \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute $g(s)=f\!\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right)$ and $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x$.
First, for $a_n{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)cos\,(n\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,d\,(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Coefficients $b_n$ (for $n \geq 1$) and $a_0$ can be found similarly.

To summarize, the Fourier series of $f$ is

$$
f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(a_n\cos\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)\right),
$$

where the coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,dx \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)sin\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
y''(x) + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = f(x), \qquad a \leq x \leq b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
\alpha_1 y(a) + \beta_1 y'(a) = \gamma_1, \qquad 
\alpha_2 y(b) + \beta_2 y'(b) = \gamma_2
$$

where $P, Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ are real constants such that $(\alpha_i, \beta_i) \neq (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y \equiv 0.$ Specifically:

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y \equiv 0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem either has no solution or a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

$$
A = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}\hspace{0.167em} {\alpha }_{1} {y}_{1} ( a ) + {\beta }_{1} {y}_{1}^{\prime } ( a ) & {\alpha }_{1} {y}_{2} ( a ) + {\beta }_{1} {y}_{2}^{\prime } ( a ) \\ {\alpha }_{2} {y}_{1} ( b ) + {\beta }_{2} {y}_{1}^{\prime } ( b ) & {\alpha }_{2} {y}_{2} ( b ) + {\beta }_{2} {y}_{2}^{\prime } ( b )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y \equiv 0$ if and only if $\det(A) \neq 0.$ In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions. So, setting $\alpha_i = 0, \beta_i = 1, a = 0,$ and $b = \pi,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{y}_{1}^{\prime } ( 0 ) & {y}_{2}^{\prime } ( 0 ) \\ {y}_{1}^{\prime } ( \pi  ) & {y}_{2}^{\prime } ( \pi  )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y = e^{m x}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m = \pm 4\textrm i.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
y_1(x) = \cos 4x, \qquad y_2(x) = \sin 4x.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
y_1'(x) = -4\sin 4x, \qquad y_2'(x) = 4\cos 4x.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot 0) & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot 0) \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \pi ) & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \pi )\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(A)| & =|0\cdot 4-4\cdot 0| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(A) = 0,$ the corresponding homogeneous BVP $\textrm{has infinitely many solutions}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}-3y\} & =L\{2{u}_{\pi /2}(t)\cdot sin\,(2t-\pi )\} \\ L\{{y}^{′}\}-3L\{y\} & =L\{2{u}_{\pi /2}(t)\cdot sin\,(2t-\pi )\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $\mathcal L\left\{y' \right\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=-2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{y' \right\}  = sY(s) - y(0)   = sY(s) + 2
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
2u_{\pi/2}(t)\cdot \sin\!\left(2t-\pi\right)
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $f(t)=2\sin(2t-\pi).$ This can be interpreted as time-delayed sinusoidal forcing. 

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
\mathcal L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\} = e^{-as} \cdot \mathcal L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\pi )\} & ={e}^{-(\pi /2)s}\cdot L\{2sin\,(2\,(t+\frac{\pi }{2})-\pi )\} \\  & ={e}^{-(\pi /2)s}\cdot L\{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\} \\  & ={e}^{-(\pi /2)s}\cdot 2\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{-\pi s/2}}{{s}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}

$$"] [:db/cas 17592186228953 :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution $y_p$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where $u_1$ and $u_2$ satisfy the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′} &=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
u_1(x)=-\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f(x)y_2(x)}{W(y_1,y_2)}\,\mathrm{d}x,
\qquad
u_2(x)=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f(x)y_1(x)}{W(y_1,y_2)}\,\mathrm{d}x,
$$

where $W(y_1,y_2)$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)=\tan x.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
y_c(x)=A\cos x + B\sin x.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
y_1(x)=\cos x,
\qquad
y_2(x)=\sin x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are linearly independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =\begin{vmatrix}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={y}_{1}(x){y}_{2}^{′}(x)-{y}_{1}^{′}(x){y}_{2}(x) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ are independent.

Let’s compute $u_1(x)$ and $u_2(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =-\int \operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-ln\,|\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x| \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =\int \operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx \\  & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-ln\,|\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x|)+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡xln\,|\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x|.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\,\underbrace{-\,\operatorname{cos}⁡xln\,|\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x|}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)=-\cos x\ln\!\left|\tan x+\sec x\right|.
$$" "Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution $y_p$ using the ansatz

$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{8{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+8{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

The determinant of $P$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}det(P)=2\cdot 1-1\cdot 1=1,\end{aligned}
$$

 however, $P$ is not orthogonal since, for example, the first column is not normalized.

$$

$$

$$

$$

and $Q-I$ is not singular since, for example, it doesn't have proportional rows or columns.

Therefore, for the approximate distribution of $X$, we obtain

$$
X \mid ∼N(nμ, nσ^{2}); ∼N(110 \cdot 3, 110 \cdot \frac{4}{3}); ∼N(330, \frac{440}{3})
$$"] [17592186188000 :question/worked-solution "Recall that the central limit theorem states the following:

$$"] [17592186188023 :question/worked-solution "For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta = \theta_0$ if

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta_0)}{x'(\theta_0)}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
y'(\theta_0) \neq 0 \qquad \textrm{and}\qquad x'(\theta_0) = 0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at $\theta_0$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\dfrac00$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
\lim\limits_{\theta \to \theta_0^{-}} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \pm\infty \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \lim\limits_{\theta \to \theta_0^{+}} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \pm\infty.
$$

In this case, we're told that $y'\left(\dfrac\pi2\right)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta = \dfrac\pi2$ into the expression for $x'(\theta),$ we get

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$"] [17592186189359 :tutorial/content "Suppose $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a distribution with population mean $\mu$ and population variance $\sigma^2$. Let's define a new random variable as the sum of all $X_i$'s as follows:

$$
X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

The sample mean $\overline{X}$ is given by

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
n\cdot \overline{X} =\sum_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

Therefore, our random variable $X$ is simply the product of $n$ with the sample mean:

$$
X = n\cdot \overline{X}
$$

Now, the central limit theorem (CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n$, the distribution of $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
$$

Therefore, since

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline X] = \mu, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\overline X] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}
$$

we can calculate $\textrm E[X]$ and $\textrm{Var}[X]$ using the properties of mean and variance as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X] &= E[nX^(―)] \\
&= n \cdot E[X^(―)] \\
&= nμ \\
\operatorname{Var} [X] &= \operatorname{Var} [nX^(―)] \\
&= n^{2} \cdot \operatorname{Var} [X^(―)] \\
&= n^{2} \cdot \frac{σ^{2}}{n} \\
&= nσ^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\overline{X}$ is (approximately) normally distributed, we have that $X$ is also approximately normal. Therefore,

$$
X\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2)
$$

This is an important result. It tells us that provided that we have a sufficiently large I.I.D. sample, the sum of the elements from that sample is approximately normally distributed with mean $n\mu$ and variance $n\sigma^2$. Recall that the slope of the tangent (in terms of $\theta$) is given by

$$

$$"] [17592186189391 :tutorial/content "So, it seems that the curve $r = 1+\cos\theta$ has a horizontal tangent at $\theta = \pi.$ However, to be sure of this, we need to check that the tangent lines flatten out as we approach $\theta = \pi.$ In other words, we need to check that

 

$$
\lim\limits_{\theta \to \pi} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = 0.
$$

Let's now verify that this is true:

Using techniques discussed in previous lessons, it's straightforward to show that

$$
x'(\theta)=-\sin\theta(2\cos\theta+1), \qquad 
y'(\theta)=2\cos^2\theta +\cos\theta - 1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{2{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1}{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1)}\right) \\  & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{2{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1)}\right) \\  & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{2{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{2{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\right).\end{aligned}
$$

We already know that substituting $\theta = \pi$ gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac00,$ so evaluating this limit by direct substitution won't work. However, we can evaluate this limit using L'Hopital's rule.

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{2{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{(2{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)^{′}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′}}\right) \\  & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi }\left(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi } \\  & =\frac{4\cdot (-1)\cdot (0)+0}{2\cdot 1+(-1)} \\  & =\frac{0}{1} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\lim\limits_{\theta \to \pi} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = 0
$$

we conclude that our curve does indeed have a horizontal tangent at $\theta = \pi.$
